Localizing analytic sources without analytic cutoffs

Original exposition and proofs: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. CC0.

An analytic function cannot be a nontrivial compact cutoff. Nevertheless, an analytic functional carried by a union of real compact sets can be divided into pieces carried by those sets. The construction takes place one dimension higher: multiply its harmonic field by a smooth cutoff, then solve an equation to remove the resulting Laplacian. A second use of harmonic approximation lets us assemble data whose differences eventually concentrate near a smaller carrier, even when their sizes grow without bound.

Write for the entire-test functionals with a bound on every complex neighborhood of the compact carrier , as in Analytic tests and real carriers, Definition (A1). All pairings are complex linear. We work with , , , and the positive Laplacian .

The needed approximation and solvability results already have full programme proofs in Fundamental solutions, continuation and approximation: B0–B2 for compact partitions and smooth completeness, Theorems 1.2–1.3 for regularity and limits, Theorem 4.1 for Runge approximation on arbitrary open sets, and Theorem 5.1 for exact distributional solvability on arbitrary open sets. These apply to the Laplace fundamental solution from Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, Theorem 1.1. Its power or logarithmic formula is real analytic away from zero: around a positive squared radius, the convergent binomial or logarithmic series gives the local analytic expression. Smooth right sides therefore have smooth solutions by the same Theorem 1.2.

We also use the entire odd harmonic lift, recovery formula, full harmonic converse and smallest-real-carrier theorem in Recovering analytic data from harmonic fields, Theorems 2, 4–6. The exact local holomorphic approximation is Theorem 4 of Analytic tests and real carriers. Compact cutoffs and scalar calculus are proved in metric foundations, Sections 12–13; Cauchy bounds are in complex contours, CX7–CX11 and CMI6–CMI8. The finite partition construction, immediately before Theorem 1.1, will also be used.

The smooth cutoff was applied to a harmonic function on a punctured space. It was not multiplied into an arbitrary analytic test. The correction restores precisely the equation that multiplication disturbed.

Why these tubes permit harmonic approximation

Lemma 5 (the complement condition with all components retained). Let be nonempty and compact, and put Every harmonic function on is a limit there of functions harmonic on . An odd function can be approximated by odd ones.

Proof. The exact condition in the earlier Runge theorem prohibits a nonempty compact relatively open-and-closed piece of Suppose such a piece exists and take . Choose a nearest . The segment has distance at most from . It does not meet before : any earlier meeting would be closer to than its chosen nearest point. Thus the whole half-open segment lies in (R2). Its connectedness and relative clopenness keep it in . Compactness of would then put its endpoint in , a contradiction. This argument does not require finitely many components or regularity of the boundary of .

Apply the full Runge theorem with , and . To preserve oddness, replace every approximant by . Reflection preserves both domains. For a symmetric compact set and a fixed derivative order, the error after this replacement is no greater than the previous maximum error on that set; signs from differentiating the reflection have modulus one. General compact sets may first be enlarged by their reflections.
